summary.text: A 59-year-old woman presented with severe long-term restless legs syndrome after pramipexole and pregabalin had to be stopped because of side effects. At presentation she was treated with a rotigotine dopamine-agonist patch. Table 3 lists acetylsalicylic acid, an antacid, L-DOPA, magnesium, rotigotine and tramadol at the start of BP treatment.

Baseline polysomnography showed low sleep efficiency (the value differs between table and text), many arousals with an arousal index of 22 per hour, many short wakefulness phases with frequent movement, few periodic limb movements and light obstructive sleep apnea.

She started add-on BP 50% tablets, four tablets per day, without changing other medication. Follow-up polysomnography about 2.5 months later under treatment showed clear improvement in sleep architecture, sleep efficiency 90% and a very low PLMS index of 1 per hour. She reported marked improvement in RLS symptoms and sleep, with severe restless phases and sleepless nights still occurring from time to time.

summary.text: A 65-year-old woman presented with severe insomnia and panic attacks while treated with trimipramine, and had prediabetes and cardiovascular disease. Her restless legs in the evening and at night began in late childhood and slowly worsened. Table 3 lists amlodipine, bisoprolol, candesartan, cymarin and rivaroxaban at the start of BP treatment.

Baseline polysomnography showed disturbed sleep architecture with a high prevalence of periodic leg movements, a PLMS index of 76 per hour, and IRLS was 28 of 40. After the baseline PSG she stopped trimipramine spontaneously, and RLS symptoms reduced with IRLS falling to 20 of 40.

She then started BP 50% chewable tablets, 0-0-3-3. After 2 months she described significantly better sleep, less restless-legs suffering early in the night, less awakening and a more restorative morning; IRLS fell from 20 to 9 of 40 and the PLMS index from 76 to 41 per hour.

summary.text: A 53-year-old woman presented with insomnia, likely related to psychophysiological factors, and fatigue after 10 years of sleep problems while regularly taking low-dose lorazepam. She also had RLS (IRLS 18/40), previously worse on mirtazapine and better on pramipexole and currently untreated, and stumbled and fell once a week. Table 3 lists doxylamine/valerian.

At the first consultation she was told to stop lorazepam, which she did. Four weeks later baseline polysomnography showed markedly fragmented sleep architecture. BP 50% chewable tablets, six per day, were recommended to her.

After 2 months of well-tolerated BP treatment no major changes were seen in objective PSG outcomes, perceived insomnia or restless leg discomfort, although she reported that symptoms varied markedly. Falling episodes became less frequent and she managed without any benzodiazepine, which she viewed positively.

summary.text: A 59-year-old man with no medical history and on no medication presented with severe sleep problems, low sleep quality and daytime sleepiness. He had typical RLS (IRLS 20/40), woke frequently at night and had difficulty falling asleep again because of restless legs.
PSG showed severely fragmented sleep architecture due to frequent periodic leg movements, with a PLMS index of 88 per hour. Treatment with BP 50% tablets, four tablets per day, was initiated.

Approximately two months later he reported significantly better night sleep, no further RLS symptoms (IRLS 2/40) and better restedness in the morning. PSG comparison showed sleep efficiency improved from 67% to 88%, arousals fell from 78 to 21 per hour and the PLMS index fell slightly from 88 to 73 per hour.

summary.text: A 41-year-old woman who had multiple sclerosis for about 9 years presented with chronic insomnia, worse over the last 1.5 years, while treated with citalopram for previous depression. RLS had been found about one year before and her husband reported nocturnal leg movements. She had lactose intolerance; Table 3 lists citalopram, natalizumab and riboflavin.

RLS symptoms occurred about five times per week (IRLS 20/40), subjective sleep quality was low and PSG showed disturbed sleep architecture with a high PLMS index of 30 per hour. She did not want the 50% chewable tablets and accepted BP 33% tincture at 0-0-20-20 drops per day.

After 2 months she felt better during the day and RLS symptoms at night were rare, with IRLS falling from 20 to 10 and the PLMS index from 30 to 20 per hour. She still woke at night when she forgot a dose. Fourteen months later she was still regularly taking the tincture and was very positive about the effect.
